The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Roman seabream (Chrysoblephus laticeps) averaged 5% [GSI = 5%] across reproductively active females during the peak spawning period at a water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Histological examination of ovarian biopsies confirmed that individuals at this GSI were actively undergoing vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation, indicating that the index accurately reflects imminent spawning readiness. Over consecutive sampling years the GSI of 5% [GSI = 5%] was a consistent benchmark for identifying gravid females in this population at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Future work should explore whether this index varies with female age or body condition, as such variation could refine our understanding of reproductive investment in this commercially important reef fish.

Juvenile Roman seabream undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching the size threshold associated with reproductive maturation. Based on extensive sampling across the species' core distribution along the South African south coast, the standard length at which 50% of individuals exhibit macroscopic gonadal development is 18.1 centimeters [Lp = 18.1 centimeters]. This length correlates strongly with a wet weight at puberty of approximately 105 g [Wwp = approximately 105 g]rams, a relationship derived from length-weight regressions calculated from over 800 specimens. Males and females appear to mature at similar lengths, with no statistically significant sexual dimorphism detected in the size-at-maturity relationship. The attainment of this size typically occurs during the third or fourth year of life, depending on local environmental conditions and food availability. Individuals that mature earlier than average tend to exhibit reduced growth trajectories thereafter, suggesting a trade-off between early reproduction and ultimate body size that may have implications for lifetime fecundity.

The ultimate standard length attained by Roman seabream, based on records from both commercial catches and dedicated research surveys, reaches approximately 50 centimeters [Li = approximately 50 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger sparids on the Agulhas Bank. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults averages 2222 g [Wwi = 2222 g]rams, a body size that places Chrysoblephus laticeps among the larger members of the sparid assemblage in the region. Growth increment data derived from otolith annuli reveal that the majority of asymptotic size is achieved within the first decade of life, after which annual growth slows considerably. The length-weight relationship used to derive this mass estimate follows the standard allometric equation commonly applied to sparids, and the resulting value of 2222 g [Wwi = 2222 g]rams is consistent with the heaviest individuals recorded in fishery-independent trawl surveys. Attaining such a large body size likely confers advantages in terms of fecundity and competitive dominance on the reef, though it also exposes older individuals to a longer period of potential fishing mortality.

The wet weight at birth for Roman seabream, derived from the diameter of fully hydrated oocytes, is estimated at approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams], an extremely small initial mass that is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts. This value was calculated from an assumed egg diameter of 750 micrometers, a figure reported for the congener Acanthopagrus berda and considered applicable to Chrysoblephus laticeps given the similarity in reproductive mode and egg morphology across these closely related sparids. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva, weighing just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching before transitioning to exogenous feeding on small zooplankton. This tiny birth mass necessitates a high relative growth rate during the early larval phase to reduce the high mortality risk associated with prolonged planktonic duration. Understanding this initial mass is critical for parameterizing larval transport models and for predicting recruitment variability under changing oceanographic conditions.

Maximum recorded longevity in Roman seabream, as determined from sectioned otoliths of individuals collected during long-term monitoring programs, reaches 23 years [am = 23 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 8395 days [am = approximately 8395 days], is comparable to that documented for other slow-growing, late-maturing sparids inhabiting temperate r at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]eef ecosystems. The oldest individuals in the dataset were all females, suggesting that differential mortality between sexes may contribute to the female-biased sex ratio observed among larger size classes. The thermal conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] under which these longevity records were recorded reflect the average sea surface temperature across the species' core habitat on the Agulhas Bank, and any sustained warming of this environment could potentially alter both growth rates and maximum lifespan. Future studies should examine whether individuals living at the cooler edge of the species' range exhibit extended lifespans consistent with the temperature-dependence of metabolic processes.
